9698.t: From the Hebrew phrase עמנו אל (“God is with us”) from עם (“with”) with the 1st person plural ending ־נו, and אל (“God”).

9690.t: Traditionally taken as a nominal formation from εἰλέω (eiléō, “to turn, wind”) (< *ϝελ-νέ-ω (*wel-né-ō)) with a suffix -ιξ (-ix), as seen also in ἧλιξ (hêlix, “of the same age”), χόλιξ (khólix, “guts”), δέλφιξ (délphix, “tripod”), further from…

9656.t: From ἐκτείνω (ekteínō, “I stretch out”) + -σις (-sĭs), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + τείνω (teínō, “I stretch”).

9691.t: Present stem from the e-grade of Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).

9684.t: From earlier ϝέπος (wépos), from Proto-Hellenic *wékʷos, from Proto-Indo-European *wékʷos, from *wekʷ- (“to speak”). Cognates include Sanskrit वचस् (vácas) and Avestan 𐬬𐬀𐬗𐬀𐬵- (vacah-).

9665.t: From ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “I show, present”, from ἐν- (en-) + φαίνω (phaínō)) + -σις (-sĭs).

9666.t: From ἐμφύω (emphŭ́ō, “implant”) + -τος (-tos), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + φύω (phŭ́ō, “bring forth, produce”).

9686.t: From ἔρομαι (éromai). Akin to Old Norse raun (“trial, experience”).

9604.t: Uhlenbeck and others consider it cognate with Sanskrit रम॑ते (rámate, “to calm down; to enjoy; to have sex with”), Lithuanian rimti (“calm down”), Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌼𐌹𐍃 (rimis, “tranquility”), which all come from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rém-e-ti with *h₁rem- (“to…

9658.t: From ἐλαύνω (elaúnō, “to strike”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

9605.t: From ἔριφος (ériphos, “young goat, kid”) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive suffix).

9667.t: Unknown. Schwyzer compared Sanskrit सनर (sanara), of uncertain meaning.

9687.t: No etymology. Being in the same semantic field of δοῦλος (doûlos), Beekes does not dismiss a Pre-Greek, in view, also, of the suffix -ιθ- (-īth-).

9606.t: From the root of ἐρυθαίνω (eruthaínō, “to dye red, make blush”) and ἔρευθος (éreuthos, “redness, flush”) + -μα (-ma). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”).

9674.t: Nominal formation in -σις (-sis) from ἐντυγχάνω (entunkhánō, “to meet with”).

9647.t: From rare ἐγκύω (enkŭ́ō, “to be pregnant”) + -ος (-os), from ἐν- (en-, “in-”) + κύω (kŭ́ō, “to conceive”).
